opus-5.5.text:
I think mathematics is unusually well suited for this for a few reasons. The first is that it's a domain where verification is relatively cheap compared to generation. If a model produces an answer to a hard problem, especially one with a definite numerical or closed-form answer, you can check whether it's right without needing an expert to spend weeks reading through it. That gives you a clean, objective signal, which is surprisingly rare. In a lot of other domains, like open-ended research or strategy, it's hard to say whether the model actually did well or just produced something that sounds plausible.

The second reason is that really hard mathematics genuinely requires long chains of reasoning. You can't solve a research-level problem by pattern matching to something you've seen before or retrieving a memorized fact. You have to set up the problem, try approaches, notice when they fail, backtrack, combine ideas from different areas, and keep track of a lot of intermediate structure. That's exactly the kind of sustained, coherent reasoning over many steps that we care about when we ask whether AI systems can do serious intellectual work.

And third, mathematics has a very wide range of difficulty. You can go from high school competition problems all the way up to problems that would take a professional mathematician hours or days, or even open problems. So you get a smooth ladder for measuring progress. That was part of the motivation behind building benchmarks like FrontierMath: we wanted problems that were hard enough that existing models would score very low, guess-proof so a model couldn't stumble onto the answer, and checkable automatically.

There's a broader point too. If AI systems become capable of doing frontier mathematics, that's a decent indicator they can do the kind of careful, multi-step reasoning that underpins science and engineering more generally. It's not a perfect proxy, since math is cleaner and more self-contained than the messy real world, but it's one of the best places we have to see that capability emerge in a measurable way.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think mathematics is attractive for a few reasons. One is that it's a domain where verification is relatively cheap and clean. If a model produces a proof, you can check it, and in the limit you can formalize it in something like Lean and have a proof assistant tell you whether it actually goes through. That's quite different from a lot of other domains where you might have a model produce a long piece of work and it's genuinely hard to tell whether it's correct or whether it just looks plausible.

The second reason is that math has this natural structure where problems come in a very wide range of difficulties, and the hardest ones really do require sustained reasoning over many steps. If you look at research-level mathematics, a proof isn't something you produce in one shot. You try an approach, it fails, you figure out why, you go back, you build up lemmas, you connect ideas from different areas. That's exactly the kind of long-horizon, agentic work that we care about measuring, because it's what we'd expect to be the bottleneck for AI doing useful scientific or economic work more generally.

And the third thing is that it's a domain where there's a fairly clear sense of what the frontier looks like. We know what competition math looks like, we know what graduate-level problems look like, we know what open research problems look like. So you can construct benchmarks that span that range and actually track progress in a meaningful way, rather than having everything saturate very quickly. That's part of the motivation behind something like FrontierMath, where we worked with research mathematicians to write problems that are genuinely hard, that take experts hours or days, and that aren't just retrievable from the training data.

So the combination of being verifiable, having a long tail of really difficult problems, and being structured in a way that resembles real intellectual work makes it, I think, one of the better testbeds we have. It's not perfect, and math isn't the economy, but it's a place where you can get a relatively clean signal about whether these systems can do the kind of extended, self-correcting reasoning that matters.

astra-6.text:
Mathematics is useful because you can have problems that require a very long sequence of steps, while still having a fairly precise way of checking whether the final result is correct. In many other domains, it’s difficult to distinguish a genuinely successful solution from something that just sounds convincing. With mathematics, especially when you’re working with formal proofs, you can check that each step follows from the previous ones.

And the challenge isn’t just producing lots of steps. You have to choose useful intermediate goals, work out which approaches are promising, and sometimes abandon an approach when it doesn’t get you anywhere. That makes it a good setting for testing whether a system can sustain coherent reasoning toward a distant objective.

There’s also a broad range of difficulty, from fairly routine exercises to open research problems. So you can investigate how performance changes as the required reasoning becomes longer and more demanding. It doesn’t capture everything we care about in intelligence, but it gives us a relatively clean setting in which to study those capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
Mathematics is useful because you can have problems that require very long chains of reasoning, while still having a precise way to check whether the result is correct. In many other domains, evaluating a long sequence of decisions is itself quite difficult. With mathematics, particularly when you use formal proofs, you can check each step with a proof assistant.

And there’s a real distinction between making a locally plausible step and making progress toward a proof. You might need to introduce a useful lemma, explore an approach, realize it doesn’t work, and backtrack. That makes it a good setting for testing whether a system can maintain a coherent strategy over many steps, rather than just produce a convincing-looking short answer.

You also have problems spanning an enormous range of difficulty, from exercises that take a few minutes to research problems that take years. So it gives you a way to study how far a system’s ability to reason extends as you give it more time and computation.
